The power curve applied to the wind speed MEASURED at each unit. This is the operational baseline that carries responsibility.
It only means something once a target HAS been declared. Without one it is not "on plan" but "there is no plan to compare against".
A type that is not declared still goes through the breakdown\n normally, stating plainly that it has no baseline — not declared is\n NOT the same as declared as 0.
The percentage of the resource baseline this loss type is allowed to consume. Taken from the design file (PVsyst, PVGIS) or from the O&M contractor's commitment.
The resource baseline less the actual less the total attributed. It is NOT spread across the columns to make the chart add up neatly — a large residual is information, not a presentation flaw.

%(n)d/%(t)d samples had wind ABOVE the curve's range — there is no telling whether the machine shut down for a storm or the curve simply stops there, so they are not added to the baseline; the resource baseline is LOWER than reality by exactly that much

Auxiliary power and overnight consumption are NOT losses — the plant uses them deliberately. They are still deducted from saleable energy, but kept apart: lumping them into losses blames operations for something operations did nothing wrong about.

The loss register answers "how much was lost". Declare an expected level here and it also answers the more important question: "is that a lot or a little" — whether soiling taking 2.1% is good or bad can only be known against a baseline.

A percentage of a small number is noise rather than signal: a windless day generating only 11 MWh turns a 3 MWh difference into 30%, and those 3 MWh say nothing about operations. It only counts as worth looking at when the residual exceeds 5% AND the resource baseline reaches at least 10% of the plant's whole-day capability.

Declared per plant, because two plants three hundred kilometres apart have quite different soiling, and each project's design file (PVsyst, PVGIS) already states its own figure. Record the basis too, so there is something to argue with the contractor from later.

The model cannot explain this part — it is NOT spread
                        across the columns to make the chart add up neatly. A
                        large residual usually comes from one of three things: the
                        outage log is incomplete, the power curve no longer
                        matches a degraded machine, or the wind measured at the
                        nacelle differs from the wind reaching the blades.
